logline: A multi-threaded drama tracing how Purdue Pharma manufactured the opioid crisis - from a Virginia mining town doctor and his patients to the DEA agents and prosecutors closing in on the Sackler family.

renewal.note: Dopesick was produced as an eight-episode limited series adapting Beth Macy's non-fiction book. No second season has been announced.

bollymeter.basis: 89 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 73 critics, an 8.6 on IMDb, and 14 Emmy nominations including a win for Michael Keaton establish this as the definitive dramatic treatment of the opioid crisis; the show's willingness to empathize with every layer of a systemic catastrophe distinguishes it from issue-drama peers.

pull_quotes.text: Strong performances from Keaton and Dever and an empathetic approach to the very real people impacted by the opioid crisis make for harrowing drama.

seasons.review_body: Dopesick premiered on Hulu October 13, 2021, and concluded November 17, 2021. It earned an 89 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes from 73 reviews, with an average of 7.7 out of 10. The series runs three timelines at once: a Virginia mining community where Dr. Samuel Finnix begins prescribing OxyContin, the DEA and federal prosecutors building a case against Purdue Pharma, and Purdue's boardroom where the Sackler family manages the crisis. The show pairs committed turns from Michael Keaton and Boyd Holbrook with a persistent sense of restraint, even as it refuses to simplify the moral architecture of the story. Its 8.6 IMDb score and 94 percent audience score also point to strong viewer reception. Michael Keaton won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Limited Series from 14 total nominations.

episode_reviews.title: First Bottle
episode_reviews.review_body: Dopesick's premiere establishes its three-timeline structure efficiently: Dr. Samuel Finnix (Michael Keaton) treating miners in Lee County, Virginia; Purdue Pharma sales representative Betsy (Kaitlyn Dever) beginning her push into Appalachian hospitals; and the DEA investigators (Rosario Dawson) building the case against Purdue years later. Creator Danny Strong's adaptation of Beth Macy's book sets up the core argument - that OxyContin's description as a less addictive opioid was a knowing pharmaceutical fabrication - without the didacticism that would have made it a lesser series. The premiere's tonal achievement is establishing sympathy for everyone in the early stage of the crisis: Dr. Finnix prescribes OxyContin to a miner with a genuine back injury out of genuine medical care, and the episode honours that good faith before the subsequent episodes demonstrate what the Sackler family knew when they brought the drug to market. Dopesick received a Metacritic score of 78 and 87 percent on Rotten Tomatoes.

The three-timeline structure is established efficiently, and the show's core argument - that OxyContin's design as a 'less addictive' opioid was a knowing pharmaceutical fabrication - is set up without the didacticism that would have made it a lesser series.

episode_reviews.title: Hammer the Abusers
episode_reviews.review_body: Dopesick's finale delivers legal and personal reckonings across all three timelines without providing the false catharsis that the subject matter's dramatic scale would normally demand. The Sackler family faces consequences that feel both real and insufficient in the specific way that mirrors the actual legal record - settlement without admission, accountability without proportionality. Michael Keaton's final scenes as Dr. Finnix are the episode's most emotionally precise achievement: a convergence of professional ruin and personal survival that the show accumulated eight episodes of specific detail to earn. The finale's treatment of the opioid crisis' actual legal outcome - Purdue Pharma's 2020 guilty plea - was identified by reviewers as the episode's most politically honest choice: refusing to dramatise a resolution more satisfying than the one that actually happened.

The Sacklers face consequences that feel both real and insufficient, mirroring the actual legal record. Dr. Finnix's arc reaches a quiet resolution that lands as the series' most earned emotional moment.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Finnix's final scene, a convergence of professional ruin and personal survival that the show earns across eight episodes of accumulated detail.
